phenomenon.subcategory: Andean underworld deity / syncretic devil figure

description.summary: Supay is a significant deity in Andean (Inca/Quechua) mythology who rules the underworld realm Ukhu Pacha; originally an ambivalent god of death, he was recast by Spanish colonial missionaries as equivalent to the Christian devil, a syncretic transformation that persists in modern Andean culture.
description.full: Supay (also spelled Zupay, Çupay, or Supai) is one of the most significant supernatural entities in Andean mythology, serving in the pre-Columbian Inca religious system as the deity presiding over Ukhu Pacha — the inner world or underworld realm beneath the earth. The Inca cosmos was divided into three realms: Hanan Pacha (the upper world), Kay Pacha (the middle world of living humans), and Ukhu Pacha, with Supay as its ruler. Originally, Supay was not inherently evil but was understood as an ambivalent force — a necessary counterpart governing death and mineral wealth. He could protect the dignified dead while tormenting others, embodying balance between opposing forces. This nuanced pre-Columbian understanding was fundamentally altered during the Spanish colonial period (beginning 1532), when Catholic missionaries, particularly Fray Domingo de Santo Tomás and subsequent chroniclers, reinterpreted Supay as equivalent to the Christian devil to facilitate conversion. The Quechua word for Supay — meaning 'shadow,' 'soul,' or 'death' — was repurposed as the translation for 'devil' in early Quechua catechisms, fundamentally demonizing the indigenous deity. Today, Supay is syncretically understood throughout the Andean region as both a feared underworld entity and a powerful protective spirit propitiated for mineral wealth. In Bolivian mining communities, he merges with the figure of El Tío, a deity of the underground who must be appeased with offerings to ensure miner safety. The Diablada dance at the Carnaval de Oruro in Bolivia features Supay as the principal devil figure, a dramatic fusion of pre-Columbian and Catholic traditions.

etymology.origin: Quechua language of the Andean peoples. The name derives from the Quechua root 'supa,' documented by Spanish chroniclers as meaning shadow, illness, death, or soul/anima.
etymology.meaning: Shadow, soul, illness, death; in colonial usage reinterpreted as 'devil'
etymology.first_use: Documented in early colonial Quechua-Spanish vocabularies, notably by Fray Domingo de Santo Tomás (1560). Pre-Columbian oral use is older but undated.

features.description: Depicted with large, curving horns — a feature reinforced by syncretic association with the Christian devil image
Some depictions show a feline or animalistic face with extended fangs
Depicted with large or elongated ears in some traditional representations
Eyes described as glassy and penetrating in some accounts

physical.morphology: As a multiform deity, Supay can assume any appearance. His appearance was significantly shaped by colonial-era Christian iconography, merging indigenous underworld deity imagery with the European devil figure. In the Diablada dance, Supay is represented by elaborate masked costumes with horns, demonic faces, and wings.

abilities.description: Can move freely between Hanan Pacha (upper world), Kay Pacha (middle world), and Ukhu Pacha (underworld)
As a multiform deity, can assume any appearance including that of holy figures
Described as a trickster figure who questions everything, manipulates beliefs, and can transform holy figures into evil ones
In mining communities, Supay/El Tío is believed to control access to mineral wealth underground; proper propitiation brings good ore yields

behavior.diet: Not described as feeding in the conventional sense; receives offerings of coca leaves, cigarettes, alcohol, and llama blood in mining contexts
patterns: Demands ritual propitiation from miners before they enter the earth
Punishes those who fail to make proper offerings or show disrespect
Orchestrates misfortune and abundance in equal measure depending on relationship with humans
Associated with seasonal festivals, particularly the Carnaval de Oruro

range.description: The Andean region of South America, encompassing the territories of the pre-Columbian Inca Empire. Strongest contemporary presence in mining communities of Bolivia and Peru.

hotspots.notes: The Carnaval de Oruro, recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, features the Diablada dance in which Supay plays the central antagonist role

first_recorded.source: Pre-Columbian Andean oral tradition; first documented in Spanish colonial sources of the 16th century, including Fray Domingo de Santo Tomás's Vocabulario (1560) and Inca Garcilaso de la Vega's Comentarios Reales (1609)

temporal.seasonal_patterns: The Carnaval de Oruro, featuring Supay in the Diablada, takes place annually in February/March (before Lent)

origins.cultural_roots: Supay originates in the Andean cosmological system of the Quechua-speaking peoples and the Inca Empire. In the pre-Columbian framework, Supay was a legitimate and necessary deity governing death and the underworld — not an evil figure but an essential force in cosmic balance.
origins.earliest_accounts: The earliest written accounts are in Spanish colonial chronicles of the 16th century. Fray Domingo de Santo Tomás's Vocabulario de la lengua general de todo el Peru llamada lengua Qquichua (1560) is among the earliest lexicographic sources documenting the term. Inca Garcilaso de la Vega's Comentarios Reales de los Incas (1609) and Guamán Poma de Ayala's Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (c. 1615) provide further early documentation.
origins.folklore_connections: The colonial demonization of Supay represents one of the most dramatic examples of religious syncretism in South American history. The process parallels similar transformations of indigenous deities across Mesoamerica and the Caribbean under Spanish colonialism.

timeline.significance: Start of the colonial transformation of Supay's meaning

history.modern_era: Today, Supay persists most vigorously in Bolivian and Peruvian mining communities, where he is syncretized with El Tío — the underground lord to whom miners make offerings of coca leaves, cigarettes, and alcohol before beginning work. This propitiation reflects a pragmatic relationship: the miners simultaneously fear Supay and depend on his goodwill for safety and ore yield. In the Carnaval de Oruro, the Diablada dance represents Supay's forces of evil being defeated by the archangel Michael, dramatizing the colonial-era theological overlay on a pre-Columbian deity.

documentary.name: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno
documentary.description: Chronicle by Guamán Poma de Ayala documenting Andean religion and Spanish colonial religious practices; one of the primary indigenous-authored sources touching on Supay.
documentary.analysis: Essential primary source for Andean religious concepts; written by an indigenous chronicler with both Christian and traditional Andean perspectives.

paranormal.name: Genuine underworld deity
paranormal.description: Traditional Andean view: Supay is a real cosmic entity who rules the underworld and controls access to the earth's mineral wealth; proper ritual propitiation is essential for mining safety and abundance.
proponents: Traditional Andean and Quechua belief systems
evidence_cited: Continued propitiation practices in active mines

scientific.name: Colonial religious syncretism
scientific.description: Academic interpretation: Supay represents a pre-Columbian Andean deity whose character was fundamentally altered by Spanish colonial missionaries who mapped Christian devil imagery onto the indigenous death-god, producing a syncretic figure that serves both traditional and Christian theological functions.
evidence_cited: Colonial-era linguistic documentation showing deliberate reinterpretation of 'supay' as 'devil'
Comparative analysis of pre-Columbian and colonial sources

Bolivian mining community propitiation of El Tío/Supay
Carnaval de Oruro Diablada dance tradition
stories: Lake Titicaca flood myth: Supay encouraged people to disobey mountain gods and seek sacred fire, resulting in divine punishment with a great flood
Supay as creator: in some traditions, created humanity in his image, though they became 'terrible demons'
Mining propitiation: miners must make offerings to Supay/El Tío before entering the earth, or face accidents and death
folklore.beliefs: In traditional Andean belief, Supay governs the dead and the mineral riches of the earth. Mining communities maintain active ritual relationships with Supay through El Tío — offering coca leaves, alcohol, cigarettes, and llama blood at the mine entrance. The relationship is pragmatic and respectful rather than purely fearful: Supay is a powerful entity who must be honored, not merely avoided.

indigenous.significance: Supay is a central figure in Andean cosmology, reflecting the indigenous understanding of death, the underworld, and the relationship between humans and the earth's interior. His transformation through colonialism is a defining example of how indigenous religious figures were demonized to facilitate conversion.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Supay's current form reflects centuries of colonial religious imposition. Pre-Columbian Andean understanding of Supay was fundamentally different from the colonial devil figure; conflating the two erases the complexity of Andean cosmology.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Engage with academic and indigenous scholarship on Andean cosmology rather than popular demonological sources; recognize the colonial history embedded in current representations.
